etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English felen, from Old English fēlan, from Proto-West Germanic *fōlijan.

definitions.definition: (transitive, copulative) To become aware of through the skin; to use the sense of touch on.
(transitive) To find one's way (literally or figuratively) by touching or using cautious movements.
(intransitive) To receive information by touch or by any neurons other than those responsible for sight, smell, taste, or hearing.
(intransitive) To search by sense of touch.
(heading) To use or experience the sense of touch.
(transitive) To experience an emotion or other mental state about.

quote.citation: 1738, [Alexander Pope], “Stanza X”, in The Universal Prayer. […], London [actually Edinburgh]:  […]  [Thomas Ruddiman] for R[obert] Dodsley, […], →OCLC, page 6:
quote.text: Teach me to feel another's VVoe; / To hide the Fault I ſee; / That Mercy I to others ſhovv, / That Mercy ſhow to me.

quote.citation: 1910, Emerson Hough, chapter I, in The Purchase Price: Or The Cause of Compromise, Indianapolis, Ind.: The Bobbs-Merrill Company, →OCLC:
quote.text: Captain Edward Carlisle, soldier as he was, martinet as he was, felt a curious sensation of helplessness seize upon him as he met her steady gaze, her alluring smile ; he could not tell what this prisoner might do.

quote.citation: 2013 August 10, Lexington, “Keeping the mighty honest”, in The Economist, volume 408, number 8848:
quote.text: British journalists shun complete respectability, feeling a duty to be ready to savage the mighty, or rummage through their bins. Elsewhere in Europe, government contracts and subsidies ensure that press barons will only defy the mighty so far.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To think, believe, or have an impression concerning.

quote.citation: 1613 (date written), William Shakespeare, [John Fletcher], “The Famous History of the Life of King Henry the Eight”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act IV, scene ii]:
quote.text: They promised me eternal happiness; And brought me garlands, Griffith, which I feel I am not worthy yet to wear.

quote.text: When Timothy and Julia hurried up the staircase to the bedroom floor, where a considerable commotion was taking place, Tim took Barry Leach with him. He had him gripped firmly by the arm, since he felt it was not safe to let him loose, and he had no immediate idea what to do with him.

definitions.definition: (intransitive, copulative) To experience an emotion or other mental state.

quote.citation: 1897 December (indicated as 1898), Winston Churchill, chapter V, in The Celebrity: An Episode, New York, N.Y.: The Macmillan Company; London: Macmillan & Co., Ltd., →OCLC:
quote.text: Then we relapsed into a discomfited silence, and wished we were anywhere else. But Miss Thorn relieved the situation by laughing aloud, and with such a hearty enjoyment that instead of getting angry and more mortified we began to laugh ourselves, and instantly felt better.

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To sympathise; to have the sensibilities moved or affected.

definitions.definition: (heading) To sense or think emotionally or judgmentally.
(transitive) To be or become aware of.
(transitive) To experience the consequences of.
(copulative) To seem (through touch or otherwise).
(transitive, US, slang) To understand.

quote.citation: 2002, “Work It”, in Under Construction, performed by Missy Elliott:
quote.text: Shoot, errbody have the zipper jacket / And half of these thugs have the glove to match, ya feel me?

definitions.definition: (archaic) The sense of touch.

quote.citation: 1838, John Burns, The Principles of Surgery, volume 1, page 330:
quote.text: It begins as a firm elastic swelling, which communicates to the feel the idea that a fluid is contained under a firm fascia  […]

definitions.definition: A perception experienced mainly or solely through the sense of touch.

quote.citation: 1902, John Buchan, The Outgoing of the Tide:
quote.text: And then something in the sound or the feel of the waters made him look down, and he perceived that the ebb had begun and the tide was flowing out to sea.

quote.citation: 2010, Nathan Bowers, 4-H Guide to Training Horses, page 111:
quote.text: The unshanked snaffle bit is good for bending and getting a horse used to the feel of a bit.

definitions.definition: A vague mental impression.

quote.citation: 2010, Paul Wilson, “Khotan (Hetian)”, in The Silk Roads: A Route & Planning Guide‎[2], 3rd edition (Travel), Trailblazer Publications, →ISBN, →OCLC, page 379:
quote.text: You can arrange camel trips into the desert but to really get a feel for this allow yourself a couple of extra days and be prepared for what at times can be an uncomfortable journey: Xuan Zang tells us that as he left Khotan he was ‘attacked by tornados which bring with them clouds of flying gravel’.
